summary: Systematic Investor episode: Katie Kaminski and Niels Kaastrup-Larsen review 2026 trend performance, geopolitical risk and inflation (her Copenhagen talk), the AQR inflation/risk-mitigation paper and Quantica's 'Paid for Presence'. Conclusions: geopolitical risk foreshadows inflation and makes bonds/60-40 vulnerable; trend and commodities respond to different inflation regimes; trend returns come from a few big months and investors lose return by timing it.

coverage.note: Opening: geopolitical risk foreshadows inflation (teaser), intros, AI chat; view that chaos is good for managed futures
AI aside; Q4 2026 trend performance, energy/bonds/currencies; 2022 vs 2026 comparison; hedged themes
Trend risk-off vulnerability, narrative pivots, 60/40 trauma; index performance numbers Oct 2026; start of Copenhagen talk
Talk structure; geopolitical risk literature and the news-based GPR index
Findings: GPR priced, firm effects, GPR foreshadows inflation; perfect storm with AI and issuance; institutional inertia
60/40 vulnerability, Bonds Behaving Badly findings, 800-year bond data
Bond bias vs trend standards, risk parity losses, yield level, global macro under-positioned short bonds
Discretionary difficulty of reversing, rules-based neutrality, trend bond history; transition to papers
Crisis alpha definition, RMS framework, AQR inflation paper design and main results
Insurance/behavior problem, role-in-portfolio framing, AQR threat definition
AQR exhibit on inflation components, first/second responder language
Commodities: passive vs active, episodic years, ETFs roll yield, index concentration; intro to Quantica paper
Quantica Paid for Presence: 20 best months, dollar-weighted vs time-weighted, public vs private funds, rebalancing
Liquidity enables timing, anonymous liquid-alt investors
Model portfolios, institutional process, access frequency and bad decisions
Institutional structure for holding trend, portable alpha with equities, rebalancing
Portable alpha payoff, bonds plus trend; book plug and outro

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's it's an ideal time for managed futures. So we like chaos.
claims.claim: Managed futures benefit in a chaotic geopolitical and inflationary environment, so 2026 was seen as an ideal year for them.
claims.testable: partly: depends on defining chaos with a measurable proxy

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's still dominated by energy, of course, and you know, one or two of the currencies also making some moves,
claims.claim: Trend performance in Q4 2026 was driven mainly by energy plus yen and euro trends, while bonds rallied against what he believed was widespread short-bond positioning among trend peers.
claims.testable: partly: CTA positioning data would be needed

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: trend is such a weird strategy that it's just lat- latching onto the biggest prevailing themes.
claims.claim: Trend following latches onto the biggest prevailing market themes, so a year being good for trend does not mean it resembles earlier good years.
claims.testable: yes: compare trend sleeve exposures across years

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it feels actually like a nice relatively hedged trend environment this year
claims.claim: In 2026 the AI-driven equity uptrend and the inflation/geopolitics-driven fixed income and energy trends offset each other in timing, giving trend a diversified, hedged year.
claims.indicator: equity trend, bond trend, energy trend
claims.conditions: two dominant themes that work at different times of year
claims.testable: partly: cross-theme correlation of trend sleeves

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it was geopolitical risk, so the energy trade was similar. That's true. But the bond story was a little different, and the equity story was completely different.
claims.claim: 2026 resembles 2022 only in the energy trade; the bond and equity stories differ, so the analogy is weak.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: a risk off move, that is probably the most dangerous for trend following at this point
claims.claim: A sudden risk-off move is the biggest threat to trend following in late 2026 because trend is positioned long equities from the AI boom and short bonds.
claims.conditions: trend long equities and short bonds after the AI-boom and inflation themes
claims.testable: partly: need trend positions and reversal episodes

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: we had very strong trends last year and they pivoted to being long energy
claims.claim: Trend themes rotate: last year's de-dollarisation and bond trends pivoted in March toward long energy and a different bond narrative, so the dominant theme is not stable.
claims.testable: partly: sleeve return attribution by year

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you have one bad year and then people feel completely traumatized
claims.claim: A single bad year (2022) for 60/40 traumatises investors even after decades of good results, which biases them against reconsidering the portfolio rationally.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Societe Generale Trend up 57 basis points in October up 16.47.
claims.claim: Trend indices were up roughly 15.7 to 16.5 percent year to date in October 2026 (BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend), within a hair of each other, while the short-term traders index was only up 5.6 percent.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders index, Trend barometer 50

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Just underscoring the US's importance in terms of driving this very narrow rally in in equities.
claims.claim: In 2026 the MSCI World gained 12.45 percent but EAFE only 8.72 percent, showing the equity rally is narrow and driven by the US; the world government bond index was down about 3 percent.
claims.indicator: MSCI World, MSCI EAFE, S&P 500, World Government Bond Index

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: they basically create this and there's even a Bloomberg ticker where you can look at the overall level of geopolitical risk.
claims.claim: A news-article-based geopolitical risk index (Iacoviello and co-authors, LLM/AI-based version) measures geopolitical risk, split into oil/energy, threats versus actions and by country, and is available on Bloomberg.
claims.indicator: Geopolitical risk index (Caldara-Iacoviello GPR, AI-based GPR), Bloomberg ticker

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it has been increasing in the more recent period and we've seen some shocks in geopolitical risk that are sizable.
claims.claim: Measured geopolitical risk has trended up recently with large shocks such as the US-Iran conflict.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: geopolitical risk does seem to be priced.
claims.claim: Geopolitical risk is priced in markets: it is a systematic risk that investors bear and are compensated for, meaning a risk premium exists.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: certain companies are more exposed to this than others, especially those with international trade exposure
claims.claim: Geopolitical risk has real firm-level effects that vary by company, with companies exposed to international trade more affected.
claims.testable: yes: firm-level sorts on trade exposure

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: over 100 years of data across 44 different countries that geopolitical risk foreshadows [snorts] inflation
claims.claim: A January paper using over 100 years of data across 44 countries finds geopolitical risk leads inflation.
claims.testable: yes: lead-lag regression of GPR on CPI

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: when you have geopolitical risk, especially on the supply side, um you will end up with a inflation risk premium or structural inflation premium.
claims.claim: Supply-side geopolitical risk produces a structural inflation risk premium that is currently being repriced in markets, which should make bond investors nervous.
claims.indicator: inflation risk premium, breakevens, bond yields
claims.testable: partly: inflation risk premium needs a model estimate

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's it's like a perfect storm, which to me makes it well, one more interesting, but it might also make the traditional portfolios a lot more vulnerable for a lot longer time
claims.claim: Oil-driven higher rates, heavier Treasury issuance, AI-driven corporate demand for capital and AI energy demand together form a perfect storm that could keep traditional portfolios vulnerable for a long time.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: We know it's so difficult to change our minds about how we do things including how we invest.
claims.claim: Investors and investment committees find it hard to change how they invest, so portfolios stay anchored to past regimes even when conditions change.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: But when you add geopolitical risk, deglobalization and other threats, actually your portfolio becomes vulnerable.
claims.claim: A 60/40 portfolio is well diversified in a low-inflation, low-geopolitical-risk world, but becomes vulnerable when geopolitical risk, deglobalisation and other threats are added.
claims.conditions: low inflation regime works; inflationary/geopolitical regime fails

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: bonds, A, tend to co-move sometimes with stocks when inflation is a key risk
claims.claim: Bonds tend to move with stocks (positive stock-bond correlation) when inflation is the key risk, as in 2022 and often over the last five years.
claims.testable: yes: rolling stock-bond correlation vs inflation

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: bond volatility is elevated when inflation is higher
claims.claim: Bond volatility rises when inflation is higher (seen in 2022 and partly in 2026).

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: bonds lose their safe haven status when inflation is high and stocks are down
claims.claim: Bonds fail as a safe haven when inflation is high and stocks fall, because inflation is a natural predator of bonds.
claims.indicator: bond returns in equity drawdowns split by inflation level

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: Alex Grezerman and I did in over 800 years and we say, "Ooh, bonds are good, but they're they're vulnerable to to to inflation."
claims.claim: Testing bonds over very long histories (800 years) rather than only the recent decades shows bonds are good but vulnerable to inflation, which corrects the bias of recent data.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they implemented a kind of a I think a leverage risk parity strategy or some sort um pretty much at the low of interest rates.
claims.claim: A Danish public pension fund adopted a leveraged risk-parity-type strategy near the low in interest rates and suffered massive losses as rates rose.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the 10 12 year deck you know period after year 2000 where bonds or sorry equities were underwater
claims.claim: Investors tolerate equities or bonds going 5 to 12 years without new highs yet treat a trend fund 1 to 2 years below its high-water mark as a catastrophe, an inconsistent standard.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: I said bonds are great if the yield's high enough.
claims.claim: Bonds are a good holding when yields are high enough, so the answer to bond weakness is not to hold no bonds but to buy when the yield compensates for risk.
claims.conditions: if a risk-off move follows, high yields add attraction

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of global macro firms actually had a pretty good narrative about why bond yields should go higher. But then when you looked at their books and their exposure, they had very little short bond exposure.
claims.claim: In 2022 many discretionary global macro funds had the right narrative for higher yields but held very little short bond exposure, an example of discretionary bias to what worked.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: can you imagine how difficult it would be to go from you know, buying the dip for 25 years every time and now suddenly having to short the highs every time.
claims.claim: A JGB trader describes how hard it is for a discretionary investor to move from buying dips for 25 years to shorting highs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's just this complete you know, agnostic view as to whether we should be long or short. We just follow the rules
claims.claim: A rules-based strategy has no view on direction, so it can be short bonds as easily as long, which is an underappreciated benefit for a total portfolio.
claims.testable: yes: compare symmetric rules vs discretionary

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: It didn't work well at all whenever we shorted in most of the history of Trend and we got accused for having long ball bond bias.
claims.claim: For most of trend's history short bond positions did not pay because of the secular bond bull market, so trend was accused of having a long-bond bias.
claims.testable: yes: long/short split of bond trend P&L

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: If bonds just go back to being absolutely lovely, Trend's going to be back long again.
claims.claim: Trend has no fixed bond bias: it flips back to long bonds whenever bonds start trending up again.
claims.direction: long bonds if bonds trend up

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you need to be unbiased. So be aware of your biases. You need to be opportunistic.
claims.claim: Crisis alpha (profit during market stress) requires three traits: unbiased, opportunistic and liquid; today's stresses are inflation and geopolitical risk, not the same as past ones.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: risk mitigation, they have the first responders, so things that react immediately to a shock. Then they have the second responders, which is trend that kind of likes difficult environments, and then diversifiers.
claims.claim: The risk-mitigation framework classes assets as first responders (react instantly to a shock), second responders (trend, reacts over weeks to months) and diversifiers (robust), and the portfolio needs each for geopolitical and inflation threats.
claims.testable: partly: classify strategies by response time in event studies

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: We're going to look at inflation at different perspectives, both rising inflation, stable inflation, falling inflation
claims.claim: The AQR paper studies assets and strategies across rising, stable and falling inflation, since different inflation regimes need different protection.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: they show how commodities really work when inflation is spiking, but maybe not in a deflationary and other environments.
claims.claim: Commodities work when inflation spikes but not in deflationary or other environments.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: trend is the one strategy in here that is the most robust to and likes inflationary uh periods, including deflationary periods, uh more than any of the other investments that they looked at.
claims.claim: In the AQR study price trend is the strategy most robust across inflationary and deflationary periods, more than other investments.
claims.indicator: trend strategy returns by inflation regime

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: many of the more classic investments like private equity, equity, they were very vulnerable to to an inflationary shock and changes in inflation.
claims.claim: Private equity and equities are very vulnerable to inflation shocks and to changes in inflation.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Um it's too late to buy it after the hurricane.
claims.claim: Protection is typically wanted only after the event, so like insurance it must be bought before, even though trend does not cost money over time.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you understand the role of an investment in your portfolio, you might have a higher chance of holding it.
claims.claim: Defining each holding's role (first responder, second responder, diversifier) makes investors more likely to hold it through bad periods and avoids reacting after the fact.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if we change the threat not to just equity drawdowns, but to inflation as as a key risk because we're holding a lot of bonds
claims.claim: The risk-mitigation question should be asked against inflation as the threat, not only equity drawdowns, because portfolios hold many bonds and equities can be hurt by a big enough inflation shock.
claims.testable: partly: define hedge targets by threat

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: And they show how uh correlation to inflation changes um you know, across different types of um components like headline inflation, core, food, energy.
claims.claim: AQR's exhibit shows sensitivity of assets and strategies (60/40, Treasuries, equities, commodities, gold, price trend, economic trend) to headline inflation and its components core, food and energy, with price trend looking robust across them.
claims.indicator: headline, core, food, energy CPI components vs asset and trend returns

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: So you have someone that shows up first and it seems to be your commodities when it's inflation. And then you have something that shows up second and that seems to be trend, right?
claims.claim: In an inflation shock commodities are the first responder and trend the second responder.
claims.testable: partly: timing of response in events

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: a passive allocation to commodities over time is not very good risk-adjusted returns.
claims.claim: A passive commodity allocation has poor long-run risk-adjusted returns; active commodity risk or trend are better ways to obtain commodity exposure.
claims.testable: yes: Sharpe of passive index vs trend

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: that's where you see like the big years either down or up are opportunity sets
claims.claim: Commodity returns are episodic: 2014 (down), 2022 and 2026 were good for trend, and the big up or down years are the opportunity set.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: commodities aren't bonds. They're not very safe. They're very volatile. They do have the correlation properties we like
claims.claim: Commodities have the inflation correlation wanted but, unlike bonds, no positive carry and high volatility, so they need active management to avoid extreme outcomes.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there are some really, really um challenging ways some of these ETFs are put together. Uh it has to do with roll yields
claims.claim: Commodity ETFs can perform poorly because of roll yield costs and their construction, so implementation needs expert care.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: a lot of the the indices are very energy focused. So, you might end up having a very undiversified commodity exposure
claims.claim: Commodity indices are heavily weighted to energy, so index exposure is undiversified (e.g. little wheat exposure when wheat moved in summer 2026).

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: the average return and trend was about 5.6% over a huge horizon. But they said if you took out the 20 largest months
claims.claim: Quantica finds trend's average return of about 5.6 percent falls to about minus 0.5 percent if the 20 largest months are removed, so a few shock months dominate returns.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it was about 1.7% or I think it was around four something percent was the typical dollar invested return
claims.claim: Dollar-weighted investor returns in trend were well below the 5.6 percent index return (about 4 percent, speaker unsure), because investors exit after underperformance and buy after strong periods.
claims.indicator: dollar-weighted vs time-weighted returns, fund flows

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: this effect was much more present in public funds than in private funds.
claims.claim: The timing penalty is larger in liquid public funds than in private funds, where investors cannot trade.
claims.indicator: public vs private fund investor returns

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: they tend to kind of use more rebalancing strategies instead. So, okay, we've made some money, let's rebalance into equities.
claims.claim: Institutions that hold a trend allocation for long use rebalancing (take profit into equities, add after drawdowns), which may do as well as or better than the index.
claims.direction: rebalance gains to equities, add to trend after losses

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the fact that you can actively trade it is sort of a hindrance that it causes people to kind of be more focused on short-term
claims.claim: Liquidity lets investors trade their trend allocation and focus on the short term, whereas illiquid assets hide drawdowns and force holding.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that liquidity, combined with the fact that those investors, for the most part, are anonymous to us
claims.claim: Daily-liquid ETF and mutual-fund trend products have anonymous investors the manager cannot coach through drawdowns, which may worsen timing behavior.
claims.testable: partly: flows into liquid vs institutional vehicles

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's really the firms that are providing those model portfolios, similar to the consultants in the institutional space, that need to kind of need to help with that narrative.
claims.claim: Model portfolio providers now carry the role of helping end investors hold managed futures, so managers must supply them with information.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: Maybe it's a new CIO change or some sort of like other shock that causes those type of re-evaluation or change in board, you know, constituency, change in consultant.
claims.claim: Institutions change allocations mainly through governance events such as a new CIO, board or consultant change.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: the frequency that you have access to those decisions can increase the probability of adverse decisions, and that's exactly what day trading research tells us
claims.claim: The more often investors can act on a decision, the more adverse emotional decisions they make, so slowing the process improves results.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's really about creating an understanding of the to the board and to the investment team what the expectations are, what the role is, and sort of appropriate benchmarks
claims.claim: Holding trend long-term requires target portfolios, a clear role, expectations and long-term benchmarks, including the knowledge that 20 months generated most of trend's performance.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you need the diversification, but you can't hold it separately, then actually it makes a lot of sense to combine equities with trend.
claims.claim: Combining equities with trend in one portable-alpha product suits investors who need equity-like returns and diversification but cannot hold trend separately.
claims.conditions: investors who need equity returns and cannot hold trend alone

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: buying the dip or rebalancing the strategy for trend with equities actually works reasonably well.
claims.claim: Buying the dip or rebalancing trend against equities works reasonably well, showing cohesive portfolio characteristics.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: that trend helps them not do as as badly when equities are down
claims.claim: A portable equity-plus-trend product lags equities sometimes when equities are up but is still up, and trend limits losses when equities fall.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Maybe we should really start thinking about bonds plus trend as well.
claims.claim: Portable alpha could pair bonds with trend, not just equities with trend.
